title: Continuity
lead: A function is continuous at a point when its graph has no break there. Here that idea is made exact by three conditions, the ways it can fail are sorted into removable, jump and infinite discontinuities, continuity is extended to intervals and to composite functions, and the Intermediate Value Theorem is stated for a function continuous over a closed interval.
objectives: Explain the three conditions for continuity at a point.
State the theorem for limits of composite functions.
Provide an example of the intermediate value theorem.
summary_html:
• For a function to be continuous at a point, it must be defined at that point, its limit must exist at the point, and the value of the function at that point must equal the value of the limit at that point.
  • Discontinuities may be classified as removable, jump, or infinite.
  • A function is continuous over an open interval if it is continuous at every point in the interval. It is continuous over a closed interval if it is continuous at every point in its interior and is continuous at its endpoints.
  • The composite function theorem states: If $\kf(x)$ is continuous at $\kL$ and $\lim_{x\to a}\kg(x)=\kL,$ then $\lim_{x\to a}\kf(\kg(x))=\kf\left(\lim_{x\to a}\kg(x)\right)=\kf(\kL).$
  • The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that if a function is continuous over a closed interval, then the function takes on every value between the values at its endpoints.

In the following exercises, use the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT).

Let $h(x)=\begin{cases}3x^{2}-4, & x\le 2\\ 5+4x, & x\gt 2\end{cases}$ Over the interval $[0,4],$ there is no value of x such that $h(x)=10,$ although $h(0)\lt 10$ and $h(4)\gt 10.$ Explain why this does not contradict the IVT.

answer.solution: The IVT asks for a function continuous over the closed interval, and $h$ is not continuous over $[0,4].$ At $x=2$ the first piece gives $h(2)=3(2)^{2}-4=8=\lim_{x\to 2^{-}}h(x),$ while $\lim_{x\to 2^{+}}h(x)=5+4(2)=13,$ so $h$ has a jump discontinuity at 2. The first piece runs from $h(0)=-4$ up to $8$ on $[0,2],$ and the second takes only values above $13$ on $(2,4],$ so the values between $8$ and $13,$ among them $10,$ are jumped over. Since the hypothesis of the theorem fails, it promises no $c,$ and there is no contradiction.

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, use the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT).

A particle moving along a line has at each time t a position function $s(t),$ which is continuous. Assume $s(2)=5$ and $s(5)=2.$ Another particle moves such that its position is given by $h(t)=s(t)-t.$ Explain why there must be a value c for $2\lt c\lt 5$ such that $h(c)=0.$

answer.solution: Since both s and $y=t$ are continuous everywhere, then $h(t)=s(t)-t$ is continuous everywhere and, in particular, it is continuous over the closed interval $[2,5].$ Also, $h(2)=3\gt 0$ and $h(5)=-3\lt 0.$ Therefore, by the IVT, there is a value $x=c$ such that $h(c)=0.$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, use the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT).

[T] Use the statement “The cosine of t is equal to t cubed.”

a. Write a mathematical equation of the statement.

b. Prove that the equation in part a. has at least one real solution.

answer.solution: a. $\cos t=t^{3}.$ b. Let $f(t)=\cos t-t^{3}.$ It is the difference of a trigonometric function and a polynomial, both continuous everywhere, so $f$ is continuous over $[0,1].$ At the ends, $f(0)=\cos 0-0=1\gt 0$ and $f(1)=\cos 1-1\approx 0.540-1=-0.460\lt 0.$ Since $0$ lies between $f(0)$ and $f(1),$ the IVT gives a number $c$ in $[0,1]$ with $f(c)=0,$ that is, $\cos c=c^{3}:$ the equation has at least one real solution.

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether each of the given statements is true. Justify your response with an explanation or counterexample.

$f(t)=\dfrac{2}{e^{t}-e^{-t}}$ is continuous everywhere.

answer.solution: False. It is continuous over $(-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty).$

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether each of the given statements is true. Justify your response with an explanation or counterexample.

If the left- and right-hand limits of $f(x)$ as $x\to a$ exist and are equal, then f cannot be discontinuous at $x=a.$

answer.solution: False. Equal one-sided limits mean only that $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists, the second of the three conditions; $f(a)$ may still be undefined or differ from the limit. For example, $f(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}$ of Example 2.26 has $\lim_{x\to 2^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to 2^{+}}f(x)=4,$ yet $f(2)$ is undefined, so $f$ is discontinuous at $2:$ it has a removable discontinuity there.

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether each of the given statements is true. Justify your response with an explanation or counterexample.

If a function is not continuous at a point, then it is not defined at that point.

answer.solution: False. Consider $f(x)=\begin{cases}x & \text{if}\;x\ne 0\\ 4 & \text{if}\;x=0\end{cases}.$

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether each of the given statements is true. Justify your response with an explanation or counterexample.

According to the IVT, $\cos x-\sin x-x=2$ has a solution over the interval $[-1,1].$

answer.solution: True. Let $g(x)=\cos x-\sin x-x.$ It is built from trigonometric functions and a polynomial, so it is continuous over $[-1,1].$ At the ends, $g(-1)=\cos 1+\sin 1+1\approx 2.382$ and $g(1)=\cos 1-\sin 1-1\approx -1.301.$ Since $2$ lies between $g(1)$ and $g(-1),$ the IVT gives a number $c$ in $[-1,1]$ with $g(c)=2,$ a solution of the equation.

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether each of the given statements is true. Justify your response with an explanation or counterexample.

If $f(x)$ is continuous such that $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, then $f(x)=0$ has exactly one solution in $[a,b].$

answer.solution: False. IVT only says that there is at least one solution; it does not guarantee that there is exactly one. Consider $f(x)=\cos(x)$ on $[-\pi,2\pi].$

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether each of the given statements is true. Justify your response with an explanation or counterexample.

The function $f(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-4x+3}{x^{2}-1}$ is continuous over the interval $[0,3].$

answer.solution: False. The function is rational, so it is continuous at every point of its domain, but its denominator $x^{2}-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ is zero at $x=1,$ which lies in $[0,3].$ There $f(1)$ is undefined, so $f$ is not continuous at $1$ and therefore not continuous over $[0,3].$ (Since $\dfrac{x^{2}-4x+3}{x^{2}-1}=\dfrac{(x-1)(x-3)}{(x-1)(x+1)},$ the limit at $1$ is $\dfrac{1-3}{1+1}=-1,$ so the discontinuity is removable.)

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether each of the given statements is true. Justify your response with an explanation or counterexample.

If $f(x)$ is continuous everywhere and $f(a),f(b)\gt 0,$ then there is no root of $f(x)$ in the interval $[a,b].$

answer.solution: False. The IVT does not work in reverse! Consider $(x-1)^{2}$ over the interval $[-2,2].$

exercises.prompt:
[T] The following problems consider the scalar form of Coulomb’s law, which describes the electrostatic force between two point charges, such as electrons. It is given by the equation $F(r)=k_{e}\dfrac{|q_{1}q_{2}|}{r^{2}},$ where $k_{e}$ is Coulomb’s constant, $q_{i}$ are the magnitudes of the charges of the two particles, and r is the distance between the two particles.

To simplify the calculation of a model with many interacting particles, after some threshold value $r=R,$ we approximate F as zero.

a. Explain the physical reasoning behind this assumption.

b. What is the force equation?

d. Is there any finite value of R for which this system remains continuous at R?

answer.solution: a. The force falls off as $1/r^{2},$ so far from a particle it is tiny beside the forces of the particles near it; treating every pair farther apart than $R$ as exerting no force changes the model very little and spares the calculation of the many distant pairs. b. $F(r)=\begin{cases}k_{e}\dfrac{|q_{1}q_{2}|}{r^{2}} & \text{if}\;r\lt R\\ 0 & \text{if}\;r\ge R\end{cases}$ d. No. At $r=R,$ $F(R)=0,$ while $\lim_{r\to R^{-}}F(r)=k_{e}\dfrac{|q_{1}q_{2}|}{R^{2}},$ which is positive for any finite $R$ and nonzero charges. The limit from the left never equals $F(R),$ so the force has a jump discontinuity at $R,$ whatever finite value $R$ takes.

exercises.prompt:
[T] The following problems consider the scalar form of Coulomb’s law, which describes the electrostatic force between two point charges, such as electrons. It is given by the equation $F(r)=k_{e}\dfrac{|q_{1}q_{2}|}{r^{2}},$ where $k_{e}$ is Coulomb’s constant, $q_{i}$ are the magnitudes of the charges of the two particles, and r is the distance between the two particles.

Instead of making the force 0 at R, instead we let the force be 10−20 for $r\ge R.$ Assume two protons, which have a magnitude of charge $1.6022\times 10^{-19}\;\text{C},$ and the Coulomb constant $k_{e}=8.988\times 10^{9}\;\text{Nm}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}.$ Is there a value R that can make this system continuous? If so, find it.

Recall the discussion on spacecraft from the chapter opener. The following problems consider a rocket launch from Earth’s surface. The force of gravity on the rocket is given by $F(d)=-mk/d^{2},$ where m is the mass of the rocket, d is the distance of the rocket from the center of Earth, and k is a constant.

[T] After a certain distance D has passed, the gravitational effect of Earth becomes quite negligible, so we can approximate the force function by $F(d)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{mk}{d^{2}} & \text{if}\;d\lt D\\ 10{,}000 & \text{if}\;d\ge D\end{cases}.$ Using the value of k found in the previous exercise, find the necessary condition D such that the force function remains continuous.

Recall the discussion on spacecraft from the chapter opener. The following problems consider a rocket launch from Earth’s surface. The force of gravity on the rocket is given by $F(d)=-mk/d^{2},$ where m is the mass of the rocket, d is the distance of the rocket from the center of Earth, and k is a constant.

As the rocket travels away from Earth’s surface, there is a distance D where the rocket sheds some of its mass, since it no longer needs the excess fuel storage. We can write this function as $F(d)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{m_{1}k}{d^{2}} & \text{if}\;d\lt D\\ -\dfrac{m_{2}k}{d^{2}} & \text{if}\;d\ge D\end{cases}.$ Is there a D value such that this function is continuous, assuming $m_{1}\ne m_{2}?$

answer.solution: No. At $d=D,$ $F(D)=-\dfrac{m_{2}k}{D^{2}},$ while $\lim_{d\to D^{-}}F(d)=-\dfrac{m_{1}k}{D^{2}}.$ For $F$ to be continuous at $D$ these must be equal, and for a distance $D\gt 0$ and $k\ne 0$ that happens only if $m_{1}=m_{2}.$ Since $m_{1}\ne m_{2},$ the two values differ for every $D,$ and $F$ has a jump discontinuity wherever the mass is shed.

exercises.prompt:
Prove the following functions are continuous everywhere

$f(\theta)=\sin\theta$

answer.solution: For all values of $a,f(a)$ is defined, $\lim_{\theta\to a}f(\theta)$ exists, and $\lim_{\theta\to a}f(\theta)=f(a).$ Therefore, $f(\theta)$ is continuous everywhere.

exercises.prompt:
Prove the following functions are continuous everywhere

$g(x)=|x|$

answer.solution: Take any real number $a;$ $g(a)=|a|$ is defined. If $a\gt 0,$ then $g(x)=x$ for $x$ near $a,$ so $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=a=|a|.$ If $a\lt 0,$ then $g(x)=-x$ near $a,$ so $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=-a=|a|.$ If $a=0,$ the one-sided limits are $\lim_{x\to 0^{-}}(-x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}x=0,$ so $\lim_{x\to 0}g(x)=0=g(0).$ All three conditions for continuity hold at every $a,$ so $g(x)=|x|$ is continuous everywhere.

exercises.prompt: Where is $f(x)=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if}\;x\;\text{is irrational}\\ 1 & \text{if}\;x\;\text{is rational}\end{cases}$ continuous?

answer.solution: Nowhere

exercises.prompt:
True or False. In the following exercises, justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

A function has to be continuous at $x=a$ if the $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists.

answer.solution: False. The limit existing is only the second of the three conditions for continuity at $a$; $f(a)$ must also be defined and equal to the limit. For a counterexample take $f(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}$ of Example 2.26: $\lim_{x\to 2}f(x)=4$ exists, but $f(2)$ is undefined, so $f$ is not continuous at $2$ (it has a removable discontinuity there).

exercises.prompt:
True or False. In the following exercises, justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

If $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ does not exist, then f is undefined at the point $x=a.$

answer.solution: False. A removable discontinuity is possible.<sup class="fn" data-note="c-r211-reason"></sup>

exercises.prompt: Determine the domain such that the function $f(x)=\sqrt{x-2}+xe^{x}$ is continuous over its domain.

answer.solution: $[2,\infty]$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-r225-interval"></sup>

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, determine the value of c such that the function remains continuous. Draw your resulting function to ensure it is continuous.

$f(x)=\begin{cases}\sqrt{x+1}, & x\gt -1\\ x^{2}+c, & x\le -1\end{cases}$

A ball is thrown into the air and the vertical position is given by $x(t)=-4.9t^{2}+25t+5.$ Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that the ball must land on the ground sometime between 5 sec and 6 sec after the throw.

answer.solution: The position $x(t)=-4.9t^{2}+25t+5$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous over $[5,6].$ At the ends, $x(5)=-4.9(25)+125+5=7.5\gt 0$ and $x(6)=-4.9(36)+150+5=-21.4\lt 0.$ Since $0$ lies between $x(5)$ and $x(6),$ the Intermediate Value Theorem gives a time $c$ in $[5,6]$ with $x(c)=0$: the ball is at ground level at some time between 5 sec and 6 sec after the throw.

footnotes.html: The key prints $[2,\infty];$ since $\infty$ is not a real number, the interval is $[2,\infty).$

derivations.what: the continuity of cosine and sine
derivations.source: Calculus, 2.4 Continuity, Continuity of Trigonometric Functions

assumes.text: $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous at $0$.

steps.tex: \mk{L}{\lim_{x\to a}\cos x}=\mk{a}{\lim_{x\to a}\cos(x-a)\cos a}-\mk{b}{\lim_{x\to a}\sin(x-a)\sin a}
\mk{L}{\lim_{x\to a}\cos x}=\mk{a}{\cos\left(\lim_{x\to a}(x-a)\right)\cos a}-\mk{b}{\sin\left(\lim_{x\to a}(x-a)\right)\sin a}
steps.cap: The constant factors $\cos a$ and $\sin a$ come out of the limits; $\cos$ and $\sin$ are continuous at $0$, the limit of $x-a$, so each limit passes inside them.

assumes.text: $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous at $0$.

steps.tex: \mk{L}{\lim_{x\to a}\sin x}=\mk{a}{\lim_{x\to a}\sin(x-a)\cos a}+\mk{b}{\lim_{x\to a}\cos(x-a)\sin a}
\mk{L}{\lim_{x\to a}\sin x}=\mk{a}{\sin\left(\lim_{x\to a}(x-a)\right)\cos a}+\mk{b}{\cos\left(\lim_{x\to a}(x-a)\right)\sin a}
steps.cap: The constant factors $\cos a$ and $\sin a$ come out of the limits; $\sin$ and $\cos$ are continuous at $0$, the limit of $x-a$, so each limit passes inside them.
